<meta>The previous page introduced Ficino's letter to Antonio Canisiano, setting the stage for a philosophical investigation into the nature of pleasure. Ficino distinguished between different schools of philosophical discourse, preparing the reader for a Neoplatonic synthesis. This page begins the formal treatise by examining the soul's divisions according to Plato.</meta>

## ¶ Chapter One. Concerning the parts of the soul.
## ¶ Likewise concerning gladness, joy, and pleasure, according to Plato.

<margin>P</margin>Plato, therefore (to begin with him as the leader of these philosophers), when he had divided the soul into two parts—namely, the mind and the senses—attributed **gladness** and **joy** to the mind, and **pleasure** to the senses. However, he thinks these first two differ from one another, because all joy is worthy of praise, whereas gladness is partly to be praised and partly to be blamed. For he defines gladness <note>original: "laetitia"; often used for more external or excitable mirth</note> as a certain elevation of the mind in the possession of some good things, which is able to both exceed and preserve moderation. Joy <note>original: "gaudium"; a more internal, spiritual delight</note>, however, is that very delight which is received from contemplation or some other practice of the virtues. And so, in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the soul, beauty, and love</note>, when he spoke of that first and true life which the soul enjoys in the heavenly seats, he says that it is "nourished by the contemplation of truth, and it rejoices." For this reason, he frequently calls joy the "nourishment of the mind." For he wants truth itself to be like a field, and the contemplation of that truth to be like the fruits of that field. Then, the nourishment which is taken from these two is the joy by which the mind thoroughly enjoys the contemplation of truth. 

For this reason, in the same *Phaedrus*, when he was disputing about those shadows into which the soul has been pressed down and submerged from the highest and true light, he says: "There is much effort to see where the field of truth is; for the suitable food of the soul comes from there, and the nature of the wings by which the soul is raised up is nourished by this." Plato calls these "wings" those by which the soul flies back to the things above, from where it had descended on account of the thought of earthly things. Since this can be achieved through two virtues—namely, the contemplative and the moral—Plato understands these same virtues (as I interpret him) to be the "wings" of the soul itself. These the soul recovers by the contemplation of truth and divine things, just as it had lost them through the desire for these earthly things. When, indeed, having recovered its wings through the practice of both natural and moral philosophy, it has flown back to the heavens, he thinks two rewards are given to the returning soul: one is the contemplation of divinity. The other is a certain perfect and absolute joy, which the soul enjoys in that very knowledge of God. Plato calls the former "ambrosia" <note>The food of the gods</note> and the latter "nectar" <note>The drink of the gods</note> in the *Phaedrus* with these words: "The soul which has truly beheld and been nourished by these things, entering again within the heaven, returns home. But when the charioteer has returned, standing the horses at the manger, he sets before them ambrosia, and over it nectar to drink." Following the manner of Pythagoras <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who influenced Plato's views on the soul and reincarnation</note>, he calls the "charioteer" reason. The "horses," however, are the other parts and natures of the soul which reason leads. the rest

<summary>Marsilio Ficino begins his treatise by defining the Platonic divisions of the soul and the resulting types of happiness, distinguishing between sensory pleasure, mental gladness, and spiritual joy. He utilizes the allegory of the winged chariot from Plato's Phaedrus to explain how the soul ascends to divine contemplation.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Phaedrus, Pythagoras, soul, joy, gladness, pleasure, ambrosia, nectar, charioteer, virtues, contemplation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Plato's psychology, specifically how the higher faculties of the soul are nourished by truth. It transitions from the definition of "joy" to a critique of "pleasure" (voluptas), contrasting the spiritual delight of the mind with the physical sensations of the body.</meta>

...to be led and ruled entirely. And I believe that this is what is signified by some of the more excellent poets <note>original: "vatibus"; can mean poets, prophets, or seers</note> when they mention ambrosia or nectar, or the charioteer guiding the soul. This, then, is the divine opinion of our Plato concerning the nature of joy itself. Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of sacred texts; Ficino famously translated the *Corpus Hermeticum*</note> seems to have understood this same truth when he said these things about the supreme God: “You bestow upon us reason, sense, and intelligence. Reason, so that we may track you through inquiries <note>original: "suspitionibus"; here meaning investigative conjectures or traces</note>; sense, so that we may recognize you; and cognition, so that, knowing you, we may rejoice that you have shown yourself to us in your entirety.” But enough concerning joy for now.

### ¶ Chapter II. What pleasure is, and why it is not a good in itself, for many reasons, according to Plato.

<margin>u</margin>Plato maintains that pleasure is a certain sweet motion in the senses, which arises from the fulfillment of a lack <note>original: "indigentia"; a state of being in need or empty</note>. For lack and its fulfillment are, in a certain way, opposing forces. From lack arise desire and pain, while from fulfillment, pleasure comes to our senses. He does not think this pleasure of which we are now speaking should be numbered among "the goods." Although he demonstrated this with many very true arguments, this one is the first and most powerful of all: ¶ Just as the presence of heat makes the things it touches hot, so too by the presence of "The Good," all things to which goodness is added become good. However, no one becomes better through the possession of pleasure. Indeed, pleasure exists in beasts even more than in humans, yet animals are not better than humans—they are not even "good" in a moral sense. Furthermore, women, children, and the foolish—as well as all who are cowardly—pursue pleasure and embrace it with all their might, much more so than men who are good and excellent in character. Yet it would be absurd if a "good" were more suited to the wicked and the cowardly than to honest and excellent men.

¶ Nor can opposites be mixed together, as he believes. Yet pleasure is undoubtedly found where there is evil, since it is not lacking in the wicked and the unjust. Therefore, pleasure can in no way be "The Good," because it combines with that which is evil. Since "The Good" and "The Bad" are opposites, they can never truly join together. ¶ Add to this what is said by Socrates in the *Gorgias* <note>One of Plato's dialogues focusing on ethics and rhetoric</note>: that good and evil are never found in the same man at the same time. Yet the same person, at the very same time, is frequently affected by pain and pleasure alike. For he calls every lack "painful" and every fulfillment of that lack "pleasant" to the senses. For instance, he calls thirst a lack of nature, and drinking a fulfillment. Therefore, the former is troublesome, while the latter is agreeable; to drink...

<meta>catchword: furthermore</meta>

<summary>Ficino defines pleasure as a sensory response to the filling of a physical lack, arguing that it cannot be the "Supreme Good" because it is shared by animals and the wicked. He contrasts this with "joy," which is a higher spiritual state, and uses the simultaneous experience of thirst and drinking to show that pleasure and pain coexist, unlike true good and evil.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Hermes Trismegistus, pleasure vs joy, Socrates, Gorgias, ethics, nature of the soul, fulfillment of lack</keywords>

ficino.translation:
<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding Plato’s definition of pleasure. Having established that pleasure arises from the fulfillment of a physical need, the author now uses several Platonic arguments to prove that pleasure is inherently unstable, often mixed with pain, and ultimately a hindrance to the higher functions of the mind and soul.</meta>

-># ON PLEASURE<-

<sig>Y</sig>
4

...furthermore, it happens that one can experience both [pleasure and pain] at once. From this, he <note>Plato</note> wishes to show that it is possible for someone to possess pain and pleasure simultaneously. Indeed, desire, anxiety, suspicion, envy, and pity—all of which contain pain within themselves—are companions of pleasure. For this reason, Timaeus <note>original: "timæns"; likely referring to the speaker in Plato’s *Timaeus*</note> says that desire, permitted by the senses, proceeds from pain and pleasure at the same time; thus, it happens that pleasure is coupled and confused with pain. And since good is not mixed with evil, he denies that pain (which is an evil) and pleasure can be "the good."

¶ Furthermore, since every good thing ought to be stable and permanent, who would say that pleasure—which has no stability—is a good? Yet, this cannot be denied if one considers its definition: pleasure is unstable and uncertain. For in its definition (as we recalled above), it was called a "motion" <term>motion: *motio* or *kinesis*; in Platonic philosophy, things that are constantly changing or moving are considered less "real" or "good" than things that are eternal and still</term>. Nothing is more contrary to stability than motion. Nor is there anyone who has ever tasted any pleasure of the body who does not know how fragile it is, how brief, with what speed it slips and flows away, and how quickly it is turned into its opposite. 

Moreover, that which is good can never be contrary to another good. Yet, since pleasure hinders many of the greatest goods, who could doubt that it is contrary to the good? For pleasures hinder **prudence**, they pour darkness into the mind, they corrupt judgment, and with their charms and enticements—like certain little harlots—they allure the minds of men and ensnare them. They cast the entire nature of man down into the mud and filth of vices and crimes. For the divine Plato, in his letter to Dionysius <note>Referring to the *Epistles* attributed to Plato, specifically addressed to the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse</note>, says that "pleasure brings detriment to men, giving birth to ignorance, restlessness, foolishness, and insolence." 

¶ Furthermore, there is no good that is not worthy of either praise or veneration. Yet no one of sound mind praises pleasure, nor is anyone judged worthy of honor and glory simply because they enjoy the greatest pleasures. Rather, he is honored who is of such a character that he scorns and neglects them with a high and unconquered spirit. 

¶ Added to this is the fact that no good can rightly be called "ours" unless it is either inherent in our very nature or has proceeded from ourselves. And we are nothing other than **mind and reason**. The body, however, is a **prison** <note>original: "carcer"</note> and a **tomb** <note>original: "sepulchrum"; this reflects the famous Orphic/Platonic pun *soma sema*—"the body is a tomb"</note> for us. The senses, indeed, are like certain guards or ambushers, who seem to care for and strive for this above all: to plunge us deeper into the darkness of this prison and to bind us tight, so that the souls may not fly back to their own place and heavenly homeland...

<meta>Pencil annotation "161" at bottom center</meta>

<summary>This page argues that physical pleasure is not a true "good" because it is fleeting, mixed with pain, and acts as a distraction or "prison" for the rational mind. It draws on Platonic themes to contrast the stability of virtue with the unstable "motion" of sensory pleasure.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Timaeus, Dionysius, pleasure vs. good, stability of virtue, body as a prison, dualism, prudence, sensory motion</keywords>

pymander.translation:
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s dedication to Cosimo de' Medici. After tracing the lineage of ancient wisdom (Prisca Theologia) through Hermes Trismegistus to Plato, Ficino now explains why he is dedicating this specific translation to Cosimo and provides an overview of the book's contents, known as the Pymander.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO
<meta>catchword: do se</meta>

...I thought it right, fortunate Cosimo, to dedicate this little work to your name. For since I myself, aided by your resources and amply supplied with your books, have applied myself to Greek studies, it is fitting that I offer the first fruits of my Greek studies to that same person. Nor was it right to dedicate the work of such a wise philosopher, such a pious priest, and such a powerful king to anyone, unless the person to whom it is dedicated surpassed all others in piety, wisdom, power, and all other things. Now, to descend to the writings of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij". This refers to Hermes Trismegistus, whom the Romans identified with Mercury.</note>, the title of this book is *Pymander*; for of the four persons who debate in this dialogue, the primary role is attributed to Pymander. He published the book in Egyptian letters; and, being likewise skilled in the Greek language, he communicated the mysteries of the Egyptians to the Greeks by translating them from there. The purpose of this work is to discuss the power and wisdom of God. And since their operations are twin, the first of which remains in the very nature of God, while the second extends to external things—and while the former conceives the first and eternal world, the latter gives birth to the second and temporal world—it discusses most seriously both operations and both worlds: what the power of God is, what His wisdom is, by what order they conceive internally, and by what progression they give birth externally. Furthermore, how those things which have been produced toward

<column-break/>

# PREFACE
**A 4**

each other behave, in what they agree, or in what they differ, and finally in what way they regard their author. The order of the volume is such that it is divided into fourteen small books: so that the first parts of the dialogue are given to Pymander, Trismegistus holds the second, Aesculapius the third, and Tatius <note>Tat, the son of Hermes in the Hermetic tradition.</note> occupies the fourth place. Mercury therefore intends to instruct Aesculapius and Tatius in divine matters. He who has not learned cannot teach divine things. But by human wit we cannot discover those things which are above human nature. Therefore, there is need of divine light, so that we may behold the sun itself by the light of the sun. Indeed, the light of the divine mind is never infused into the soul unless the soul itself, like the moon toward the sun, is turned completely toward the mind of God. The soul does not turn toward the mind unless it also becomes "mind" <note>Ficino is referring to the "Nous" or higher intellect.</note>. Indeed, it does not become mind before it has cast aside the deceptions of the senses and the clouds of the imagination <note>original: "phantasiæ". In Renaissance psychology, this was the faculty that processed sensory images.</note>. For this reason, our Mercury stripped away the mists of the senses and imagination and withdrew himself into the inner sanctuary <note>original: "adytum"</note> of the mind. Soon Pymander—that is, the divine mind—flows into him. From there, he contemplates the order of all things, both those existing in God and those flowing from God. Finally, he explains to other men those things which were revealed to him by the divine power.

<summary>Ficino dedicates his translation of the Pymander to Cosimo de' Medici, arguing that only a man of Cosimo's stature is worthy of Hermes Trismegistus. He outlines the Hermetic cosmology of the "two worlds" and the process of divine revelation through the silencing of the senses.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Marsilio Ficino’s dedication to Cosimo de' Medici. After tracing the lineage of ancient wisdom (Prisca Theologia) through Hermes Trismegistus to Plato, Ficino now explains why he is dedicating this specific translation to Cosimo and provides an overview of the book's contents, known as the Pymander.</meta>

# PREFACE
**Page 8**

...This, therefore, is the title of the book, its purpose, and its order. But you, fortunate Cosimo, read happily, and live long, so that it [the book] may also live long for the benefit of your fatherland.

->JACQUES LEFÈVRE D'ÉTAPLES<-
<note>original: "Faber Stapulensis." Lefèvre was a leading French humanist and theologian who edited this edition of the Hermetic corpus.</note>
->TO THE READER.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring a floral or foliate design.</image-desc>WE HAVE TAKEN CARE, with what diligence we could, to return this work in a corrected state from a corrupted copy, both out of love for Marsilio [Ficino], whom we venerate as a father, and because we are moved by the magnitude of the wisdom of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage.</note>. Furthermore, for the sake of helping students, we have added a few things by way of summaries; although we freely admit that each of the books requires greater effort for its explanation, and a talent far more outstanding than our modest strengths might suggest. Farewell.

<column-break/>

# ARGUMENT OF THE FIRST DIALOGUE.
**Page 9**

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'I' featuring a bird (possibly a swan or pelican) amidst foliage.</image-desc>IN the first dialogue, Mercury treats the Mosaic mysteries <note>original: "Mosaica mysteria." This refers to the secrets of creation found in the Book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note>. For Moses saw darkness upon the face of the abyss, and the spirit of the Lord carried over the waters: but here [Mercury] sees a terrifying shadow migrating into a moist nature—which moist nature the word of the Lord was indeed cherishing. The former [Moses] announces all things created by the powerful word of the Lord; but the latter [Mercury] asserts that that shining word, which illuminates all things—the sprout of the mind—is the Son of God. He asserts that the Father Mind and the Word of the Mind do not differ in nature; he said it was consubstantial <note>original: "consubstantiale." A technical theological term meaning "of the same substance," used here to suggest that Hermes Trismegistus understood the nature of the Christian Trinity before the time of Christ.</note>. He saw also that there is a union of these. And if you desire more fully—and if it is right to ascribe such divine knowledge to men before the fleshly veil of the Word [the Incarnation]—he saw the Son being born from the Father, and the Spirit proceeding in a miraculous way from the Father and the Son, when he said: "The Mind, however, being God, most full of the fertility of both sexes, Life and Light, with its Word, gave birth to a second Mind, the Demiurge <note>original: "opificem." A "maker" or "craftsman" who shapes the physical world.</note>." He saw too the Mind, by its exuberant fertility, stretching itself out to external things, and forming the universe according to the pattern of its own divine Word, and distributing to each its own nature according to its kind in the air, in the water, and on the earth. Soon, man was made after His own likeness and image, to whose use the Demiurge Mind subjected all sensible things. Man soon fell from the intelligible sphere <note>original: "intelligibili sphæra." The realm of pure spirit and thought, as opposed to the physical world.</note> to the sphere of bodily and lustful things; from here he also contracted the origin of the "fuel of evils" <note>original: "fomitis malorum." A term for the inclination toward sin.</note>; and finally the knot of all things was loosened (by the will of God), and man was made subject to death along with the rest. What else is here, [but] that God [is] the Word...

The text presents Hermes Trismegistus as a "pagan prophet" who anticipated Christian doctrines like the Trinity and the Fall of Man.</summary>

### MEGISTI PYMANDER, DE POTESTATE ET SAPIENTIA DEI.

Cum de rerum natura cogitarẽ, ac mentis aciẽ ad superna erigerẽ, sopitis iam corporis sensibus, quemadmodũ accidere solet ijs, qui ob saturitatem uel defatigationem somno grauati, sunt; subitò mihi uisus sum cernere quendã immensa magnitudine corporis, qui me nomine uocans, in hunc modum clamaret: Quid est ô Mercuri, quod et audire & intueri desideras? quid est qd discere atque intelligere cupis? pymander.translation:
<meta>This page continues the "Argument" or summary of the first book of the Corpus Hermeticum, comparing the Hermetic creation story to the biblical account in Genesis. It then transitions into the start of the first dialogue, the Pymander, where the narrator (Hermes) experiences a divine vision.</meta>

[I heard the] holy [voice] cry out: "Sprout, grow, and propagate all seeds and my works," which is much like the Mosaic saying: "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth." <note>original: "Crescite & multiplicamini, & replete terram." A direct reference to the command given in Genesis 1:28.</note> Soon Mercury instructs us on how the way to the Mind <term>Mind: The Latin 'Mens' (equivalent to the Greek 'Nous') refers here to the Divine Intellect or the highest spark of human consciousness that connects us to God.</term> lies open, and what evil error finally leads us away from it; he shows to whom the Mind is present as a bountiful giver of goods, and from whom it is likewise absent. He explains how, just as we fall by certain steps from an intellectual and immortal nature and degenerate into decaying things, we are also restored to that prior state of a purified mind by certain opposite steps. Let Moses be the leader of the Hebrew flock by divine decree, and let Mercury be the leader of the Egyptian flock. Now, by holy instruction, he feeds his flock, living an active life; but then, praising the Father of all things with hymns and thanksgivings, he rises into the light of the contemplative life. This is the summary of the Pymander.

<column-break/>

# THE PYMANDER OF MERCURY
### TRISMEGISTUS, ON THE POWER AND WISDOM OF GOD.
### MARSILIO FICINO OF FLORENCE, TRANSLATOR.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut drop cap 'C' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or scribe, working at a desk or table with books.</image-desc>

WHILE I WAS REFLECTING on the nature of things, and raising the sharp edge of my mind to higher realms, my bodily senses were already lulled to sleep—just as usually happens to those who are weighed down by sleep due to fullness or exhaustion. Suddenly, I seemed to see someone of immense bodily size, who, calling me by name, cried out in this manner: "What is it, O Mercury <note>original: "Mercuri." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage whom the Renaissance believed was a contemporary of Moses.</note>, that you desire to both hear and behold? What is it that you wish to learn and understand?" Then I said: "Who are you?" He replied: "I am Pymander, the Mind of divine power. See what you wish, for I will be with you everywhere." I said: "I desire to learn the nature of things and to know God." To this he replied: "Embrace me in your mind, and I will instruct you in all that you hope for."

<summary>This page concludes the introductory summary comparing Hermes to Moses and begins the Pymander, the most famous Hermetic text, where Hermes Trismegistus encounters a divine vision of the "Mind of Power."</summary>
